interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a project where you took full ownership from an ambiguous starting point to a shipped result.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I was handed a one-line brief: "our onboarding flow has too much drop-off, figure out why." No specific screens named, no hypothesis handed to me, no PM available for the next two weeks.

Rather than wait, I pulled the funnel data myself and found the sharpest drop was at the email-verification step, not the signup form itself as the team had assumed. I formed a hypothesis — the verification email was landing in spam for a meaningful fraction of users based on delivery logs — proposed a scoped experiment (switching the sending domain and adding an in-app resend option), and ran it as an A/B test over two weeks, checking in with my manager briefly at the start and end but not waiting for direction in between.

The result: verification completion went from 68% to 81%, which traced through to a measurable lift in completed signups. I wrote up the funnel finding for the team afterward so the next ambiguous "drop-off" question wouldn't start from zero.

What I'd point to as the ownership signal specifically: I never went back to ask what to do next — I found the next step myself from the data and only checked in to report progress, not to ask permission to continue.

**Testing:** whether you can drive an ambiguous problem to a shipped result independently, versus needing each step specified for you.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Ownership

interviewQuestions.question: Describe a time you noticed and fixed a problem that wasn't part of your assigned work.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
While implementing an assigned feature, I noticed the internal API I was calling silently swallowed a specific class of validation error instead of surfacing it — callers just saw an empty response and no error, with no obvious reason why. It had nothing to do with my actual ticket.

I weighed whether it was worth a detour: the fix looked small — maybe half a day — and I could tell from an internal Slack search that at least one other engineer had lost time to this exact behavior months earlier without realizing the root cause. That made it worth doing rather than just working around it and moving on.

I fixed the silent swallow to return a proper error code, wrote a short note in the team channel — "found and fixed X while working on my ticket, separate small PR, here's why" — and kept my original ticket's PR clean and unrelated to the fix. Both shipped the same day.

The judgment call I'd highlight: it wasn't scope creep because I didn't quietly expand my original ticket — I split it into its own visible, communicated change, and I made a conscious call that this specific detour was cheap and clearly valuable, which isn't true of every unassigned problem you notice.

**Testing:** whether you can recognize a worthwhile unassigned problem and act with judgment about scope, rather than either ignoring everything outside your ticket or scope-creeping silently.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Beyond the ticket

interviewQuestions.question: What's a project you're proud of, and can you separate your specific contribution from the team's overall impact?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A four-person team rebuilt our search infrastructure end to end, and the aggregate result was better relevance and lower latency. My specific ownership within that was the ranking layer — I replaced a hand-tuned scoring formula with a learned ranking model trained on historical click data.

Isolated from the rest of the project: my change specifically improved click-through on the first results page from 61% to 74% in an A/B test I designed and ran myself. That's separate from the indexing-layer latency work two teammates did in parallel — both workstreams shipped together, but the ranking improvement is the piece I designed, built, and validated independently.

I deliberately lead with that separation when I tell this story, because the team's overall result sounds bigger, but it also obscures what any one person actually did — and I'd rather an interviewer credit me accurately for the ranking model than have to guess how much of the aggregate number was mine.

If pushed further, I can also speak to the indexing work at a high level since I reviewed those changes, but I'm careful not to claim I built it — that wasn't my contribution.

**Testing:** whether you can cleanly separate your individual work from a team's aggregate result, rather than letting the bigger number stand in for your specific contribution.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Isolating impact

interviewQuestions.question: Give an example of impact you had that kept paying off on work you weren't directly involved in afterward.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I built a shared retry-and-backoff library after noticing three different services on my team had each independently written buggy, slightly different versions of the same logic — one had caused a minor outage from a missing jitter that led to a thundering-herd retry storm.

I built the library once, with the failure mode from that outage specifically covered by a test, and got it adopted by my own team first. What made it compounding rather than just a good internal tool: two teams I had no working relationship with adopted it over the following year after finding it in our internal package registry, without me pitching it to either of them. One of those teams later told me it saved them roughly a sprint of otherwise-duplicated work building their own version.

I didn't design it anticipating that spread — I built it to fix a problem on my own team. The compounding part was a consequence of making it genuinely reusable (clear API, no team-specific assumptions baked in) rather than solving it in a way that only worked for our specific services.

What I'd want an interviewer to take from this: the value kept accruing to teams I never directly worked with, well after I'd moved on to other things — which is different in kind from a project whose impact stopped the day it shipped.

**Testing:** whether you have real experience with impact that compounds beyond a single project's boundary, which is a core staff-level signal, versus only project-scoped stories.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Compounding impact
